newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss parliament agrees on economic stimulus plan.
newsitem.headline: Swiss parliament agrees on economic stimulus plan.

text.p: Switzerland's parliament ironed out final differences on Wednesday in a government economic stimulus proposal, paving the way for increased infrastructure spending designed to revive the stagnant domestic economy.
Bills approved by the upper and lower houses earmark 561 million Swiss francs in federal matching funds that Berne hopes will unleash 2.4 billion francs in spending on infrastructure projects.
The lower house must still give final approval in a formal vote later today that is considered a formality, officials said. The upper house has already given its aproval.
The tax reform side of the package also came up for debate but will not be voted on until the next regular parliamentary session in June or possibly even later.
Driven to act by six years of stgnation, the government hopes the plan will add one-third of a percentage point to gross domestic product (GDP) in 1998 and 1999 and create 24,000 jobs.

But analysts have questioned whether the programme will have any marked impact on growth or employment, tending to view the scheme more as a signal from politicians that they are taking the country's economic malaise seriously.
Under the plan, the federal government will put up the money to draw matching funds from the country's 26 cantons, thousands of local governments and private investors as well.

The focus will be on maintaining and expanding public roads, tunnels and buildings. Both houses agreed to take 100 million francs originally earmarked for maintaining buildings and spend 60 million of this on jobs training for young people.
They split the other 40 million between maintaining public buildings and subsidising the federal Commission for Promotion of Innovation and Technology.

They also struck a compromise by allowing cantons to use funds in the programme to help finance preparatory work done this year on road projects rather than work done in 1998 and 1999. The lower house wanted main projects funded by mid-1997.
The stimulus scheme also includes refitting public and private buildings for energy efficiency.

"By giving a temporary stimulus to demand, the investment programme will accelerate a recovery from economic stagnation which has lasted for six years," the cabinet had said in its proposal to parliament.
Swiss Gross Domestic Product (GDP) was flat in the fourth quarter of 1996, following seven quarters of continued declines. It is expected to grow in 1997 but at a rate below one percent.
The cabinet's proposed corporate tax reform is more disputed between left and right in the coalition.
The bill would introduce a flat tax rate of 8.5 percent on corporate earnings while abolishing a capital tax now imposed on companies.
It would also lower the issue tax, a one-time levy on the share capital of new companies issuing shares, to one percent from two percent.

To make up for some of the resulting revenue loss, the cabinet wants to reintroduce a one-time tax on new life insurance policies, a proposal hotly opposed by the country's large insurance sector and many conservative politicians.

In a bid to encourage foreign investment, parliament also liberalised rules on foreign ownership of commercial property and let foreign executives buy their homes in Switzerland without having to get official approval.
